titre: 46 chromosomes, not 48: an error confirmed by forty studies
accroche: From 1923 to 1956, at least forty studies counted 48 chromosomes in humans. The right answer, 46, was confirmed within the year.
contenu_vulgarise:
Open a biology textbook from 1950: the human being has forty-eight chromosomes, twenty-four pairs. The number is no hypothesis; it is established, recounted by numerous teams. It is wrong.

## Forty confirmations of an error

At the end of the 19th century, the first estimates range from 16 to 38 chromosomes, most authors leaning toward 24. In 1912, de Winiwarter counts 47 in the testis and 48 in the ovary. In 1921, Theophilus Painter finds the Y chromosome, missed until then, and concludes that the number is 48 in both sexes. He notes, however, that his best cells show only 46 (in 1923, according to Ferguson-Smith).

He keeps 48, and so do the others. According to the review that Malcolm Ferguson-Smith devoted in 2015 to the history of cytogenetics, at least forty studies confirm this number over the following thirty-three years. According to Sophia Balderman and Marshall Lichtman, textbooks and journals still give it in the mid-1950s, and it is taught to students until 1956.

Several researchers had nevertheless counted 46 in their preparations. They assumed their technique was faulty, so settled did the number 48 seem. A plate by Hsu, reproduced in 1953 in a book by Cyril Darlington, shows 46 chromosomes when you count them, and Levan himself believed in 48 before working with Tjio. The false figure rested less on observations than on the confidence placed in it.

## What changes in 1956

Joe Hin Tjio, a cytogeneticist of Indonesian origin who mostly studied plant chromosomes, and Albert Levan publish in 1956 in the Swedish journal Hereditas a six-page paper, “The chromosome number of man.” They count 46 chromosomes in 252 of the 256 cells examined, from fibroblasts of four human embryonic lungs.

The difference lies in technique, not in instrument. Cultured cells are treated with colchicine, which accumulates cells in mid-division. A hypotonic solution then disperses the chromosomes, and the cells are squashed between slide and coverslip to spread the chromosomes in a single plane. The effect of hypotonic treatment had been described independently in 1952 by Hsu, Makino and Hughes. None of the three counted the right number.

Ford and Hamerton confirm 46 immediately, in the journal Nature, on human meiotic chromosomes.

## Who counted what, and when

The account of these weeks is disputed. In 2006, Ulf Arnason compares three accounts, those of Levan, Tjio and Hultén, with the laboratory notebook kept in Lund. Levan's, more restrained, is compatible with every detail of the notebook. According to this examination, Levan makes his first preliminary counts of 46 chromosomes around December 20-23, 1955, and Tjio his first conclusive preparations in early January 1956, two to three weeks after his arrival from Spain on December 19.

## What the right number makes visible

The right count has an immediate consequence: it makes 46 the norm, and therefore any deviation an observable anomaly. In May 1958, Marthe Gautier and her colleagues, in Paris, see a small extra chromosome in fibroblast cultures from children with trisomy 21; the result is announced in 1958 and published in January 1959. At the same time, in Great Britain, anomalies of the sex chromosomes are found, published a few months later: a single X and no Y in Turner syndrome, two X and a Y in Klinefelter syndrome.

Once 46 is the norm, a 47th chromosome becomes an observation and no longer a counting error. Ferguson-Smith's review adds that these discoveries came as a surprise: no one believed that such major anomalies were compatible with life, and the search for other examples began.

repere.texte: In 1956, Tjio and Levan count 46 chromosomes in 252 of the 256 cells examined, fibroblasts from four human embryonic lungs. Textbooks had given 48 for several decades.
repere.source: Balderman and Lichtman, Rambam Maimonides Medical Journal, 2(3), 2011

carte.punch: For thirty-three years, at least forty studies counted 48 human chromosomes. There are 46.
carte.idee: From 1923 to 1956, at least forty studies confirm 48 chromosomes in humans. In 1956, Tjio and Levan count 46 thanks to cell culture, colchicine and hypotonic treatment, and Ford and Hamerton confirm it the same year.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Ford and Hamerton, “The chromosomes of man”, Nature, 178, 1956
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Confirmation of the number 46 on human meiotic chromosomes. Reference verified (Crossref), text not read.

quiz.question: What allowed Tjio and Levan to count human chromosomes correctly in 1956?
choix: An electron microscope that showed each chromosome in relief
Banding stains that distinguished the chromosomes one by one
Cultured cells, treated with colchicine and then dispersed in a hypotonic solution
Partial sequencing that counted the DNA molecules in each nucleus
quiz.explication: Culture, colchicine, the hypotonic solution and squashing between slide and coverslip spread the chromosomes in a single plane. The electron microscope, banding (1970s) and sequencing play no part in the 1956 paper.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What chromosome-number anomaly is observed in children with Down syndrome, according to Marthe Gautier's 1958 work?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Marthe Gautier and her colleagues observe an extra small chromosome in fibroblast cultures. A missing X corresponds to Turner syndrome, and an extra Y does not characterize Down syndrome.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did some researchers who had counted 46 chromosomes in their preparations not publish that result before 1956?
choix: They thought their technique was faulty, so settled did the number 48 seem
They were waiting for Theophilus Painter's agreement before publishing
Their cells came from animals, not humans
The journal Hereditas refused papers on chromosome number before 1956
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says that several researchers had counted 46 chromosomes but assumed their technique was faulty, so settled did 48 seem. Nothing indicates that Painter's agreement was needed, that the cells were animal, or that the journal refused anything.
